title: After nearly 6 decades on the job, this retired CBSA officer shares stories from 'the booth'

image.caption: Anne Marie Handsor worked with the Canada Border Services Agency for 55 years, with much of her time spent on the front lines of the Ambassador Bridge linking Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Mich. (Leandra Vermeulen/CBC)

blocks.text: Windsor·New

Not quite 18 when she was hired, Anne Marie Handsor helped secure the border between Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Mich., spending much of her time with the Canada Border Services Agency on the front lines at the Ambassador Bridge. Newly retired, she recalls 9/11 changes, COVID-19 crossers and celebrity encounters during her 55-year career.
'I never didn't want to go to work,' Anne Marie Handsor says, recalling 9/11, COVID-19, celebrity encounters
Windsor Morning11:17Customs worker retires after 55 years on the job
Anne Marie Handsor wasn’t quite 18 years old when she was hired to help secure the border between Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Mich.
Most of her time with the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) was spent on the front lines at the Ambassador Bridge.
Fast forward 55 years and she's finally leaving the customs booth with lots to reflect upon after retiring last week.
Not quite 18, Handsor was hired to work for Canadian customs in 1971 in Windsor. (Submitted by Anne Marie Handsor)
Handsor, a Windsor native, began her career as a customs officer in 1971 when there weren't many women working for the border agency in the region.
“I do know I was the only young female officer at that time — there were five older women,” she told CBC Radio’s Windsor Morning host Amy Dodge.
“The funniest thing that used to happen to me, when people would pull up to my booth and they would go, 'It's a female.' And I go, ‘Yeah, so what's with that?’"
She said they would then reply with, "'Well, we don't like female officers because they're too thorough,’ because they thought we asked too many questions — and we did."
After nearly 6 decades on the job, this CBSA officer shares stories from 'the booth'
The union representing Canada’s border employees called Handsor “an officer at heart.”
“She loved her job and interacting with the travelling public,” said Lisa Howe, Customs and Immigration Union (CIU) Windsor branch president.

“She was always full of stories and had so many pioneering experiences with the agency through her 55 years … and helped pave the way for women in the agency when there were very few women working at the border.”
Handsor holds a picture of herself, during the start of her career as a Canadian customs worker in the 1970s. The Windsor native recently retired after 55 years on the job. (Leandra Vermeulen/CBC)
The CBSA calls Handsor’s 55 years of service one of the longest tenures in its history.
Spokesperson Maria Bohotineanu said Handsor's career demonstrated an exceptional commitment to border security and serving Canadians.

“The CBSA is grateful for her decades of dedication, professionalism and contributions to the organization,” said Bohotineaunu. “We congratulate her on this extraordinary career milestone and wish her all the best in her well-deserved retirement.”
What’s changed over the years?

When I started, all we had was a pen and a badge, and there was no protection at all. If somebody ran the port, meaning that they didn't stop at the booth, we'd have to shout, ‘Stop at the name of the Queen,’ three times — and then we could try to catch them. Well, nobody ever caught them.Anne Marie Handsor, 55-year Canadian customs officer

“When I started, all we had was a pen and a badge, and there was no protection at all. If somebody ran the port, meaning that they didn't stop at the booth, we'd have to shout, ‘Stop at the name of the Queen,’ three times — and then we could try to catch them. Well, nobody ever caught them, but that was just something that happened.”
The fallout of Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks invoked more change for customs than any other one thing or event, according to Handsor.

“That was a frightening day that day because so many people [Canadians] work over there [Michigan]. Nurses, doctors, teachers — they were all coming back home. It was a very bad day. I'll never forget that day because we realized …. right around that time that the public … was different. The public was more dangerous than in the past. The public, they saw your uniform and they they were respectful. But that's all changed. Having the tools that we do have now, it's very necessary.”
Handsor said a “multitude” of guns are coming across the border to this day — with “five, or six or more” at a time. As for drugs, she said, they’re predominantly being hidden in commercial trucks.
Human smuggling is also frequently discovered, according to the recent retiree.

“We've seen people being smuggled underneath, holding on to tractor-trailers, coming over the bridge. That's how desperate people are to get into Canada. But this … one I'm thinking of had 11 people underneath, but they did get caught.”
Vehicles move along Windsor's Huron Church Road, which leads to the Ambassador Bridge. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)
Handsor said that when she worked at the Ambassador Bridge and specifically during her time manning the truck lane, the fumes were bad.
“I had a light blue shirt. Everyone of us at the end of the day, the black soot from the trucks that were coming out every day, our collars at the back were just black — like, you had to wash those.”
Emotional COVID-19 crossings
During the peak of COVID-19, the land border was closed between Canada and the U.S. for roughly a year and a half.
Handsor said she felt for the roughly 1,500 Canadian nurses who crossed into Michigan for work each day during the pandemic — especially during what she referred to as the “worst period.”

blocks.text: “When everybody was dying and they were putting the bodies into refrigerated trucks, the nurses would pull up to the booth and they would literally start crying because they were exhausted and they've never seen anything like this.”
A Gordie Howe bridge finale
Before she put a wrap on her nearly six-decade career, Handsor asked — and was granted — permission to work one shift at the new Gordie Howe International Bridge on her last day.

“It was nice. It was a gift to me. It is really high tech. It's really good. It's clean right now. It's a beautiful bridge. The booths are a lot bigger than the ones at the [Ambassador] bridge are, and they're clean.”

Handsor got her wish granted at the end of her career to work one shift at the Gordie Howe International Bridge, shown in this drone view with transport trucks and cars entering Canada. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)
Handsor says she contemplated retiring five years ago but wanted to wait for the new crossing to open first.

“That was what my goal … and then it was a disappointment because we were going to have an honour guard. I was part of the honour guard. Then because of Trump … not letting the U.S. open the bridge, it was scaled down. We were all hyped up … it was supposed to be like a big happy celebration.”
Her share of celebrity encounters
Handsor said she had the privilege of meeting then U.S. President George W. Bush and Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chrétien roughly one year after 9/11 — an encounter she’ll never forget.

“My boss had told me, he said, 'Be prepared because George W. Bush is known for turning around and mingling with the workers.' And sure enough, he turned around, and he took my hand and he shook it. And he said to me, ‘Thank you for the work that you do, officer.’ And I said nothing. No words came out of my mouth. I don't think I talked for two days because I was in [awe]. I just wish that I could have met [U.S. President Barack] Obama, too.”
Other well-known people she encountered were musicians Smokey Robinson, Kid Rock, Bob Dylan and Alice Cooper.
Retirement plans: Good health, good garb
Now that she has finally entered the next chapter of her life at age 73, Handsor said her focus is clear.
“I hope for good health.”
Anne Marie Handsor looks at photos of her past while working for the CBSA. (Leandra Vermeulen/CBC)
She also said she wants to give more attention to her wardrobe, now that she doesn't have to worry about wearing her work uniform five days every week.
“It was a good career. And I never actually minded ... I never didn't want to go to work.”
